claims.text: Pain for < 4 to 6 weeks: no testing unless there are red flags, a serious injury, or signs of a nonmechanical cause such as pyelonephritis.
claims.quote: Usually, if duration of pain is short (< 4 to 6 weeks), no testing is required unless red flag findings are present, patients have had a serious injury (eg, vehicular crash, fall from a height, penetrating trauma), or evaluation suggests a specific nonmechanical cause (eg, pyelonephritis).

claims.text: X-rays show disc height loss, spondylolisthesis, malalignment, fragility fractures and osteoarthritis, but not disc or nerve problems.
claims.quote: Radiographs can identify most disc height loss, anterior spondylolisthesis, malalignment, osteoporotic (or fragility) fractures, osteoarthritis, and other serious bone abnormalities (eg, those due to infection or tumors), and they may be helpful in deciding whether additional imaging studies such as MRI or CT are warranted. However, they do not identify abnormalities in soft tissue (the discs) or nerve tissue (as occurs in many serious disorders).

claims.text: Neurologic deficits from nerve root or cord compression: MRI as soon as possible.
claims.quote: Neurologic deficits, particularly those consistent with nerve root compression or spinal cord compression: MRI and less commonly CT myelography, done as soon as possible

claims.text: Possible infection: WBC count, ESR and/or CRP, MRI or CT, and culture of infected tissue.
claims.quote: Possible infection: White blood cell (WBC) count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and/or C-reactive protein (CRP), imaging (usually MRI or CT), and culture of infected tissue

claims.text: Possible cancer: CT or MRI, CBC, and possibly biopsy.
claims.quote: Possible cancer: CT or MRI, complete blood count (CBC), and possibly biopsy

claims.text: Disabling or lasting > 6 weeks: MRI or CT.
claims.quote: Symptoms that are disabling or persistent > 6 weeks: Imaging (usually MRI or CT)

claims.text: Imaging findings don't always match symptoms: many people with disc herniations have no symptoms.
claims.quote: It is important to note imaging findings do not always correlate with patient symptoms. Evidence supports that many patients with disc herniations are asymptomatic
